t.3.42.1: Having thus instructed his brother, the greatly radiant Raghunandana girded on his sword, whose hilt was made of jāmbūnada gold.
t.3.42.2: Then, taking up his bow, bent in three places and an ornament to his person, and binding on two quivers, he of lofty valour set forth.
t.3.42.3: Seeing that lord of kings rushing toward him, he, deceiving him, vanished out of fear, and then came into view once more.
t.3.42.4: With his sword girded on, he took up his bow and ran toward where the deer was. He sees it ahead of him, seeming to blaze with its beauty.
t.3.42.5: Bow in hand in the great forest, he kept watching it again and again as it ran, at times passing beyond the range of an arrow's flight, luring him on.
t.3.42.6: He saw it wary and darting about in alarm, as though leaping up into the sky, now visible and now invisible in certain new places.
t.3.42.8: By appearing and vanishing again and again, he drew Rāghava away; Kākutstha grew angry, helpless and bewildered by him.
t.3.42.7: Like the disc of the autumn moon veiled by scattered clouds, it was glimpsed for a moment, and then again it shone from afar.
t.3.42.9: Then, as if utterly weary, he rested, taking shelter in the shade on a grassy meadow, and, surrounded by the animals of the forest, he was seen not far away.
t.3.42.10: Seeing him, the mighty Rāma, resolved to kill him, fitted an arrow to his very sturdy bow, and the strong one drew it back with great force.
t.3.42.11: Aiming at that very deer, he released a blazing, radiant missile fashioned by Brahmā, which was like a flaming serpent.
t.3.42.12: That excellent arrow, like a thunderbolt, pierced violently through and split the very heart of Mārīca, who wore the form of a deer.
t.3.42.13: Then, stricken by the arrow, he leapt up to the height of a palm tree and fell down; lying on the ground with little life left, he let out a terrible cry. And Mārīca, as he was dying, abandoned that artificial body.
t.3.42.15: Pierced in a vital spot by that peerless arrow, Mārīca, giving up his life, abandoned that deer form and assumed his own rākṣasa form, enormous in body.
t.3.42.14: Knowing that the right moment had come, he then raised a cry in a voice just like Rāghava's own: "Ah Sītā! Ah Lakṣmaṇa!"
t.3.42.16: Then, struck by the arrow, he became a rākṣasa, adorned with splendid armlets and decked with every ornament, wearing a golden garland and bearing huge fangs.
t.3.42.17: Seeing that terrible-looking rākṣasa fallen upon the ground, he went in his mind to Sītā, remembering the words of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.42.18: Crying out in a loud voice, "Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!", this rākṣasa has died; having heard that, how will Sītā fare?
t.3.42.19: "And what state will the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa come to?" Reflecting thus, the righteous-souled Rāma felt the hair on his body stand on end.
t.3.42.20: Then, having slain that rākṣasa in the form of a deer and having heard his cry, Rāma was seized by an intense fear born of despondency.
t.3.42.21: Then Rāghava, having slain another spotted deer and taking its meat, hastened back, moving in haste toward Janasthāna.
